title: The undeclared
hook: ten questions the Buddha set aside, and why silence was the answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha told his son: be like the earth, which doesn't recoil from what's thrown on it. What landed on you, and did you stay wide? Day four hundred fifty-five, the end of a week.

A monk named Māluṅkyāputta is sitting alone, and he's had enough. There are questions the Buddha never answers. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it finite, or infinite? Are the soul and the body the same thing, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither? Ten questions in all. So he goes to the Buddha with an ultimatum: answer them, or I'm giving up the training and going home. It's the kind of message you type at 2am. Today, what the Buddha says back.
screen: `TEN QUESTIONS.` → `ANSWER THEM, OR I LEAVE.` → `AN ULTIMATUM.`

segments.voice: First, he asks Māluṅkyāputta a question of his own. Did I ever promise you, come and train with me and I'll answer these? No. Did you ever say, I'll train only if you do? No. Then, he says, who is walking out on whom? And then comes one of the best-known pictures in the whole canon. Imagine a man shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends bring a surgeon. And the man says: don't pull it out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a laborer? What was his name, his clan? Was he tall or short, dark or fair? What village was he from? What kind of bow was it? What was the string made of, and the feathers on the shaft? That man, the Buddha says, would die before he ever found out. So the ten questions stay undeclared, avyākata, not answered either way. Why? Not because they're forbidden, and the sutta doesn't call them meaningless. Because answering them isn't beneficial, he says. It doesn't lead to letting go, to peace, to awakening. And what has he declared? This is suffering. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Four things, all about pulling the arrow out. The sutta ends with a line worth keeping: remember what I've left undeclared as undeclared, and what I've declared as declared. Buddhist schools have discussed the ten questions for centuries since. But the silence itself is a teaching. Some questions you can carry for a lifetime without letting them stop you walking.
screen: `DID I EVER PROMISE YOU THAT?` · `THE POISONED ARROW.` · `NOT BENEFICIAL, NOT LEADING TO PEACE.` · `FOUR THINGS DECLARED.` · then, large: `THE UNDECLARED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one question unanswered. Settle and breathe. Let one big question come up, one you've chewed on: why something happened, what comes after, whether you chose right. Name it once, gently. Then, instead of answering, set it down beside you like a closed book. Return to the breath. When the question taps your shoulder, notice it, and come back. It can stay undeclared for now. The bell holds the time.
The undeclared. Ten questions the Buddha set aside, because answering them doesn't pull the arrow out. Today's word.

Your line: the undeclared. Today, let one question stay open and do the next useful thing anyway. And that's week sixty-five: the dog-duty ascetic, the trap question, how many feelings, the safe bet, before, the earth, and the undeclared. Day four hundred fifty-five.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY-FIVE: DOG-DUTY · TRAP QUESTION · FEELINGS · SAFE BET · BEFORE · EARTH · UNDECLARED`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to students who want metaphysical questions settled first, and the ten undeclared questions are discussed in many schools' commentaries and debates.

match.prompt: the poisoned arrow: tap the pairs.

myth: the Buddha said the ten questions were meaningless
the sutta says answering them isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to peace.
the Buddha had promised to answer them one day
he asks Māluṅkyāputta whether he ever promised that. he hadn't.
the wounded man in the parable asks what the bowstring was made of
the archer's caste, name, height, village, bow, string, feathers: he'd die first.

fork.setup: you're shot with a poisoned arrow. the surgeon is ready. what do you do?
options: find out who shot you first
let the surgeon pull it out
ask about the feathers on the arrow
fork.reveal: the man in the parable keeps asking about the archer and dies first. the four things the Buddha declares are all about pulling the arrow out.

original.note: Pali avyākata (also spelled abyākata): undeclared, left unexplained.

trapdoor: what you thought: the undeclared means the Buddha didn't know.
what it means: ten questions deliberately set aside, because answering them doesn't lead to peace.
what a scholar hears: MN 63, the Cūḷamāluṅkya Sutta; the same ten questions recur across the canon, and Buddhist schools have debated why they were left unanswered.

notes: MN 63 paraphrased; check the list of the archer details and the 'who is walking out on whom' line, which renders the Buddha's question freely.
